Fig. 1.
Fig. 1-A The scapular plane is defined using the glenoid center point, inferior angle of the scapula, and scapula trigonum. The glenoid plane is defined using 3 representative points placed on the surface of the glenoid fossa. Pathologic glenoid version and inclination are then measured in 3D from the scapular and glenoid fossa planes. Joint-line position is measured as the distance between the glenoid center point and the scapula trigonum. The glenoid vault model (inset) is virtually placed into the glenoid on each preoperative CT scan as a tool to define premorbid glenoid anatomy. Premorbid glenoid version and inclination are measured in 3D from the scapular plane and the plane of the glenoid vault surface. Premorbid joint-line position is measured as the distance between the glenoid vault center point and the scapula trigonum. Figs. 1-B through 1-G Representative 2D orthogonal views relative to the scapular plane are used to confirm vault model position and demonstrate premorbid (Figs. 1-B, 1-C, and 1-D) and pathologic (Figs. 1-E, 1-F, and 1-G) inclination, version, and joint-line position relative to each other. (Reproduced, with permission of Elsevier, from: Ricchetti ET, Jun BJ, Jin Y, Entezari V, Patterson TE, Derwin KA, Iannotti JP. Three-dimensional computed tomography analysis of pathologic correction in total shoulder arthroplasty based on severity of preoperative pathology. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2021 Feb;30[2]:237–49. Epub 2020 Aug 7.)

Fig. 2.
Fig. 2-A Preoperative humeral head alignment is measured in the axial (anteroposterior [AP]) and coronal (superoinferior [SI]) planes with respect to the scapular coordinate system, at the level of the glenoid center point. Best-fit sphere placement of the humeral head is performed using a validated method to define the center of the humeral head, which is used for measurement of humeral scapular alignment (HSA-AP/SI) and humeral glenoid alignment (HGA-AP/SI). HSA-AP/SI is the perpendicular distance from the humeral head center to the scapular axis. HGA-AP/SI is the perpendicular distance from the humeral head center to a perpendicular line through the glenoid center point. Both HSA-AP/SI and HGA-AP/SI are expressed as a percentage of humeral head diameter. Fig. 2-B The measurements of postoperative HSA-AP/SI and HGA-AP/SI are similar to the preoperative measurements, but the postoperative measurements are referenced to the center of the humeral head component and the center of the glenoid component. Both HSA-AP/SI and HGA-AP/SI are expressed as a percentage of humeral head diameter.

Fig. 3.
Grading of bone integration of the central anchor peg of the glenoid component on CT at a minimum of 2 years postoperatively. Fig. 3-A Grade 1 indicates central anchor peg osteolysis (CPO), with dilation seen around the central peg. Fig. 3-B Grade 2 indicates bone integration to the edges of the flanges of the central peg but not within it. Fig. 3-C Grade 3 indicates bone integration within the flanges of the central peg. Grade-2 and 3 cases were both considered to have center peg integration and were grouped together as being negative for CPO for statistical analysis, whereas Grade-1 cases were defined as positive for CPO.

Fig. 4.
Scatterplot of change in glenoid component position from the early postoperative CT (CT2) to the CT at a minimum of 2 years postoperatively (CT3) for all 152 patients. The change in glenoid component version is plotted on the x axis, and the change in glenoid component inclination is plotted on the y axis. The histograms depict the frequencies of changes in implant position on each axis. Each case is color and shape-coded according to its classification in the modified Walch system (A1, A2, B1/C/D, B2, or B3) and implant type (standard glenoid [SG] or augmented glenoid [AG] component). B1, C, and D were grouped together due to their low frequency. All symbols outside of the blue box represent cases with glenoid component shift, defined as a change in component version or inclination of  $ 3^{\circ} $ from CT2 to CT3. Symbols circled in black represent cases with evidence of central anchor peg osteolysis (CPO) on CT3. Only 15 (19%) of 78 cases with glenoid component shift had evidence of CPO. Patients with CPO had a greater absolute change in glenoid component inclination from CT2 to CT3 and a greater combined absolute glenoid component version and inclination change from CT2 to CT3 compared with patients without CPO. The cases identified with arrows had a change in component version or inclination beyond the maximum shown on the axis—i.e.,  $ >10^{\circ} $ of increased inclination (n = 3),  $ >10^{\circ} $ of increased retroversion (n = 1), or  $ >10^{\circ} $ of increased anteversion (n = 1).

Fig. 5.
Examples of shift of the glenoid component without (left panel) and with (right panel) central anchor peg osteolysis (CPO). In both examples, digital templates of the positions of the glenoid and humeral head components are superimposed on representative coronal or axial CT images made early postoperatively (red templates) and at a minimum 2-year follow-up (green templates). In the panel on the left, a standard glenoid component in an A2 glenoid shows 2.3° of inclination and -12.4° of version on the early postoperative CT (top row). On the CT scan acquired at a minimum 2-year follow-up (middle row), the glenoid component was in 7.2° of inclination and -13.1° of version, representing a change in glenoid component position of 4.9° of inclination and -0.7° of version. The digital templates from both time points are overlaid on the CT images at a minimum 2-year follow-up in the middle row to demonstrate the glenoid component shift into increased inclination. A central anchor peg grade of 3 is seen on the 2-year follow-up CT with the digital templates removed (bottom row). In the panel on the right, an augmented glenoid component in a B3 glenoid showed 10.4° of inclination and -2.9° of version on the early postoperative CT (top row). On the 2-year follow-up CT (middle row), the glenoid component was in 18.7° of inclination and -6.0° of version, representing a change in glenoid component position of 8.3° of inclination and -3.1° of version. The digital templates from both time points are overlaid on this image to demonstrate the glenoid component shift into both increased inclination and increased retroversion. A central anchor peg grade of 1, indicating CPO, is seen on the 2-year follow-up CT with the digital templates removed (bottom row).

anchors.text: Figure 1. Potential strategies that can be used to augment the complexity and functionality of magnetic nanoparticles. The particles can be functionalized with antibodies for cell targeting and selection of specific stem cell subpopulations. Moreover, they can be coupled to specific growth factors and other bioactive agents. The magnetic core can be coated with a polymeric material, allowing the simultaneous incorporation of other drugs while modulating the cellular response and degradation profile. When in contact with a cell, these magnetic nanoparticles can either attach to the surface and trigger desired intracellular signaling or can be internalized and directed towards specific organelles of the cellular machinery. All of these processes can be monitored through the attachment of imaging tags on the surface of the magnetic nanoparticles or by taking advantage of the magnetic composition of these nanoparticles. As they can be detected through techniques such as MRI.

Figure 2. Sequential magnetic fusion for the formation of a cartilage construct. (A) Sixteen spheroid aggregates were formed through the use of a network of magnetic tips, which were then placed in contact after 8 days. Spheroid fusion occurred and eight doublets were formed. At day 11, four quadruplets were formed after doublet fusion and finally at day 15, four quadruplets were fused to form the final structure. (B) Toluidine blue and safranin-O staining of the engineered construct after 28 days of culture. Reproduced with permission from [25] © John Wiley and Sons (2013).

Figure 3. Endothelial cell organization in magnetic nanoparticle–alginate and alginate constructs. After the seeding into the MNP or alginate scaffold, the endothelial cells were exposed to an alternating magnetic field (magnetically stimulated) for 7 days. The control cell constructs were cultivated in a similar incubator without exposure to a magnetic field. The cells were cultured for an additional 7 days without external magnetic stimulation. Cells are stained for F-actin (red) and nuclei (blue) after 7 and 14 days (bar: 30 mm). The greatest extent of well-organized vessel-like structures (loops) was found in MNP scaffolds exposed to a magnetic field after 14 days of cell culture. MNP: Magnetic nanoparticle. Reproduced with permission from [55].

Figure 4. Magnet-scaffold configurations suggested by Russo et al. (A) External permanent magnetic ring (EM); (B) implanted permanent magnetic pins (PM); (C) implanted stainless steel pins in the field of external magnet (EM + SS). Although these configurations were defined aimed at scaffold fixation strategies, these strategies could be easily translated and applied into scaffolds incorporated with magnetic nanoparticles, including controlled drug delivery mechanisms or cell-based approaches where magnetic nanoparticles were internalized in implanted cells.

anchors.text: Figure 1. Effect on DNA content after 72 h. Normal human chondrocytes were plated in DMEM containing 0.1% calf serum and allowed to attach and equilibrate for 24 h. In the graph above, PEF signal was applied for 30 min. At the same time as PEF treatment, physical factors were added to separate cultures providing final concentrations of IGF1 at 10 ng/mL and calf serum at 1%. The cultures were allowed to incubate for 72 h and the cell layer measured for DNA content as an index of proliferation. The data is expressed as percent of corresponding controls (n = 6). DNA content for IGF1 and PEF treatments were not significantly different. *Denotes p < 0.05 versus controls.

Figure 2. PEF signal and short-term (30 min) NO release. Normal human chondrocytes were plated in DMEM containing 0.1% calf serum and allowed to attach and equilibrate for 24 h. In one experiment (light bars) L-NAME was added to 1 mM final concentration 6 h prior to PEF signal treatment. In a second experiment (dark bars) W7 was added to 0.5 mM 2 h prior to PEF signal treatment. PEF signal was applied for 30 min. At the end of the 30-min PEF signal treatment period the culture media was measured for NO content by Griess reaction. The cell layer was rinsed with phosphate-buffered saline, extracted with sodium hydroxide, and measured for protein content. Cell layer protein was used to normalize nitric oxide content. There were no significant differences in protein content. The data is expressed as percent of corresponding controls (n=6). *Designates p<0.05 versus controls.

Figure 3. PEF signal increases short-term (30 min) cGMP generation. Normal human chondrocytes were plated in DMEM containing 0.1% calf-serum and allowed to attach and equilibrate for 24 h. In one experiment (light bars) L-NAME was added to 1 mM final concentration 6 h prior to PEF signal treatment. In a second experiment (dark bars) W7 was added to 0.5 mM 2 h prior to PEF signal treatment. PEF signal was applied for 30 min. At the end of the 30-min PEF signal treatment the cell layer was rinsed with phosphate-buffered saline, extracted, and measured for both cGMP content and protein content. Cell layer protein was used to normalize cGMP content. The data is expressed as percent of corresponding controls (n = 6). *Designates p < 0.05 versus controls.

Figure 4. PEF signal and SNP increase short-term (30 min) cGMP generation. Normal human chondrocytes were plated in DMEM containing 0.1% calf serum and allowed to attach and equilibrate for 24 h. The inhibitor LY83583 was added to 1 mM final concentration 4 h prior to PEF signal treatment or addition of SNP (an NO donor). PEF signal was applied for 30 min. At the end of the 30-min PEF signal treatment or presence of SNP the cell layer was rinsed with phosphate-buffered saline, extracted, and measured for both cGMP content and protein content. Cell layer protein was used to normalize cGMP content. The data is expressed as percent of corresponding controls (n=6). *Designates p<0.05 versus controls.

Figure 5. PEF signal and increased DNA content at 72 h. Normal human chondrocytes were plated in DMEM containing 0.1% calf serum and allowed to attach and equilibrate for 24 h. In one experiment (light bars) L-NAME was added to 1 mM final concentration 6 h prior to PEF signal treatment. In a second experiment (dark bars) LY83583 was added to 0.5 mM 4 h prior to PEF signal treatment. PEF signal was applied for 30 min. The cultures were allowed to incubate for an additional 72 h. The cell layer was rinsed with phosphate-buffered saline, extracted with sodium hydroxide, and measured for DNA content as an index of proliferation. The data is expressed as percent of corresponding controls (n=6). *Designates p<0.05 versus controls.

Figure 6. SNP and PEF effects on DNA. Normal human chondrocytes were plated in DMEM containing 0.1% calf serum and allowed to attach and equilibrate for 24 h. Cultures were treated to SNP (an NO donor) or PEF and the media was changed at various times after initiation of treatment. After the culture media was removed and replaced with fresh media, the cultures were allowed to incubate until a total time of 72 h had elapsed from initiation of treatment. The cell layer was rinsed with phosphate-buffered saline, extracted with sodium hydroxide, and measured for DNA content as an index of cell proliferation. The data is expressed as percent of corresponding controls (n = 6).  $ ^{*} $Designates p < 0.05 versus controls.

anchors.text: FIGURE 1 | The osteochondral interface and bone and cartilage zones. The osteochondral interface lies between the connecting layers of articular cartilage and subchondral bone. The articular cartilage consists of three zones: superficial zone, transitional zone, and deep zone and finishes at the tidemark. Below this lies the calcified cartilage layer. The subchondral bone is located below the calcified cartilage and consists of the subchondral bone plate and subchondral trabecular bone. Vascular channels lie within the subchondral bone.

FIGURE 2 | Differences between normal and osteoarthritic osteochondral tissues. The features of the healthy osteochondral interface are homogeneous articular surface, normal chondrocytes and vascularization of the subchondral bone. With the onset of OA, the articular surface exhibits fissures; chondrocyte hypertrophy and clusters; while cysts appear in the calcified cartilage; with increased angiogenesis and nerve growth penetrating the tide mark; and decreased bone mineral density and increased bone formation in the subchondral bone.

FIGURE 3 | Schematic representation of the signaling pathways of TGF-β and Wnt involved in joint pathophysiology. TGF-β can bind to ALK5, that activates SMAD2/3 leading to chondrocyte homeostasis (blue pathway arrows). TGF-β can also bind to ALK1, activating SMAD1/5/8 that may lead to hypertrophic phenotype of chondrocytes (red pathway arrows). Wnt binds to receptors Fz or LRP5/6 activating β-catenin synthesis. A healthy expression of β-catenin leads to bone/cartilage homeostasis (purple pathway arrows) while imbalanced β-catenin can result in an OA-phenotype (pink pathway arrows).

anchors.text: Fig. 1 The three-tiered cascade of mechanotransduction pathways in cells. The first structures influenced by mechanical stimulation are different types of mechanosensors, including pericellular matrix (PCM) and extracellular matrix (ECM) components, mechanically gated ion channels and porins (such as TRPV4 and Piezo), integrins, mitochondria, cytoskeleton, and primary cilia. Mechanotransducers include multiple types of factors, such as kinases (ROCK, PI3K-AKT, MAPK, etc.), growth factors (IGF, TGF- $ \beta $, etc.), transcription factors (YAP, GREB1, etc.), secretory proteins (RCN2, etc.), and other molecules, which are activated by mechanosensors and then alter specific downstream molecules. anchors.text: FIGURE 1 | The physiopathological role of mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake. In physiological conditions, mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake stimulates ATP production thanks to the positive regulation of three Ca²⁺-dependent TCA cycle enzymes (pyruvate dehydrogenase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and oxoglutarate dehydrogenase). In the cytoplasm glycolytic reactions convert glucose to pyruvate. The Mitochondrial Pyruvate Carrier (MPC) determines the entry of pyruvate into mitochondria, where pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) oxidizes pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle leading to the generation of reducing equivalents that feed the electron transport chain and eventually ATP production. Conversely, in pathological settings, mitochondrial Ca²⁺ overload could cause the opening of the mitochondrial Permeability Transition Pore (mPTP) eventually leading to cell death.

FIGURE 2 | Scheme of the MCU complex. The mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uniporter (MCU) is composed of pore-forming subunits (i.e., MCU, MCUb, and EMRE) and regulatory subunits (i.e., MICU1, MICU2, and MICU3). MCU and the dominant-negative isoform MCUb are assembled into tetrameric complexes that span the IMM. EMRE is the essential MCU regulator, a 10 kDa protein located in the IMM whose absence causes the loss of the uniporter channel activity. A peculiar aspect of the mitochondrial Ca²⁺ uptake is its sigmoidal response to the extra-mitochondrial [Ca²⁺]. This property is due to the presence in the IMS of the MCU regulators, MICU1, MICU2, and, nearly exclusively in the nervous system, MICU3. At low cytosolic [Ca²⁺], little Ca²⁺ enters through the channel. Upon cell stimulation, the increase in cytosolic [Ca²⁺] is sensed by the EF-hands present on both MICU1 and MICU2. Consequently, conformational changes of the regulatory subunits take place, which allows the opening of the channel leading to Ca²⁺ entry inside the mitochondria.

FIGURE 3 | Ca²⁺-dependent regulation of mitochondrial dehydrogenases. (A) The mitochondrial Ca²⁺ indirectly regulates the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) that oxidizes pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. PDC is composed of multiple copies of three components: pyruvate decarboxylase (E1), dihydrolipoate acetyltransferase (E2) and dihydrolipoate dehydrogenase (E3). In response to increased mitochondrial [Ca²⁺], the Ca²⁺-dependent isoform of pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase 1 (PDP1) dephosphorylates E1, thus triggering PDC activation. (B) Ca²⁺ directly activates the isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH). The ATP/ADP ratio negatively regulates the sensitivity of Ca²⁺ binding to IDH. (C) Oxoglutarate dehydrogenase (OGDH) is a multienzyme complex similar to the PDC. It is composed of dihydrolipoamide succinyl-transferase subunits (E2, green in the figure), oxoglutarate decarboxylase (E1, pink in the figure) and dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3, yellow in the figure). Ca²⁺-binding directly regulates the activity of the enzyme.

anchors.text: Figure 1. Schematic. (a) Illustration of persistent electrical stimulation provided by electreted sandwich-like SiO₂/PDMS composite membranes to stimulate bone defect repair. SiO₂ nanoparticles are encapsulated and electreted by a negative electric field to provide induced charges and maintain stable negative electric potential across the composite membranes, delivering persistent electrical stimulation to induce bone regeneration. (b) Implanted composite membranes act as native periosteum covering the bone defect region, providing bioactive electrical microenvironment to recruit endogenous BMSCs, facilitating their differentiation into osteoblasts, and consequently enhancing well-integrated bone formation and regeneration.

Figure 2. Fabrication and characterization of the E-S/P composite membranes. (a) Schematic of the fabrication of the E-S/P composite membranes. The  $ SiO_{2} $ electret-incorporated PDMS membranes were fabricated through layer-by-layer blade-coating. Afterward, the composite membranes were polarized and electreted. (b) Contact angles of P, S/P, and E-S/P composite membranes with varying  $ SiO_{2} $ electret concentrations. (c, d) Mechanical properties. (c) Elastic modulus and (d) tensile breaking strength of P, S/P, and E-S/P composite membranes with varying  $ SiO_{2} $ electret concentrations. (e) Surface potential change over 24 h and (f)  $ \zeta $-potential change of P, S/P, and E-S/P composite membranes with varying  $ SiO_{2} $ electret concentrations under different pH conditions.

Figure 3. Characterization of E-S/P composite membranes with 3 wt % SiO₂ electrets. (a) Representative (a1) SEM and (a2) TEM images of SiO₂ nanoparticles. (b, c) Representative surface and cross-sectional SEM images of the sandwich-like (b) pure PDMS and (c) SiO₂/PDMS composite membranes. The green and red dotted boxes indicate the enlarged surface and cross-sectional morphologies, respectively (yellow arrows indicate SiO₂ nanoparticles). (d, e) COMSOL finite-element simulation showing (d) electric potential and (e) electric-field intensity during the electret polarization of the SiO₂/PDMS composite membranes. (f, g) Surface potential change and (h, i) ζ-potential change of P, S/P, and E-S/P composite membranes with 3 wt % SiO₂ electrets over 42 days. (g, i) Surface potential and ζ-potential of P, S/P, and E-S/P composite membranes at day 42, respectively.

Figure 4. E-S/P membranes facilitate the adhesion, proliferation, and migration of BMSCs. (a) Representative immunofluorescence staining images of cell adhesion after culturing on different substrates for 12 h. BMSCs on E-S/P membranes developed a more stretched spread area and more cytoplasmic protrusions compared with those from the other three groups. (b) CCK analysis of BMSCs cultured on different substrates for 1, 3, and 5 days. (c, d) Cell migration assay. (c) Representative images of the wound healing assay for BMSCs cultured on different substrates for 0 and 24 h after staining with calcein-AM, and (d) quantitative results of the remaining scratch distance by its fraction of initial defect distance for each group. Cell migration was significantly promoted for BMSCs cultured on E-S/P membranes.

Figure 5. E-S/P membranes promote the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs. (a) ALP staining and (b) ARS staining of BMSCs cultured on different substrates. (c) OCN immunofluorescence staining of BMSCs cultured on different substrates for 7 days. Red, green, and blue fluorescence represent the Alexa Fluor 594-phalloidin-stained cytoskeleton, Alexa Fluor 488-stained OCN, and DAPI-stained cell nuclei, respectively. BMSCs on E-S/P membranes demonstrate the deepest ALP staining, and the most abundant calcium module deposition and OCN expression. (d–g) Expression of the representative osteogenic-related genes (d) RUNX2, (e) ALP, (f) Col I, and (g) OCN in BMSCs cultured on different membranes for 7 days, as determined using quantitative real-time PCR. The results were normalized to GAPDH and expressed as relative expression levels to the B group. The osteogenic-related genes were significantly upregulated in BMSCs from the E-S/P group.

Figure 6. E-S/P membranes enhance rat calvarial bone regeneration in vivo. (a) 3D reconstruction images and sagittal view images of micro-CT showing the regenerated bone around the rat calvarial defects without treatment and those treated with P, S/P, and E-S/P membranes at 8 weeks post-implantation (yellow arrows indicate the margin of the bone defects). (b, c) Quantitative analysis of the regenerated bone tissues by measuring the (b) BV/TV and (c) BMD values. (d) Representative H&E and Masson-stained histological images showing bone repair around the defects treated with different membranes (black arrows indicate the implanted membrane materials). E-S/P membranes demonstrate significantly enhanced capacity to induce bone regeneration in vivo.

anchors.text: Fig. 1. Responses of cells with different membrane properties to dcEFs. (A) A simple cell in the resting state has a negative membrane potential. (B) A cell with negligible voltage-gated conductance exposed to a dcEF. The membrane towards the anode is hyperpolarized and attracts Ca²⁺ by passive electrochemical diffusion. Consequently, this side of the cell contracts, thereby propelling the cell towards the cathode. (C) A cell with voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels (VGCCs). Channels near the cathode (depolarized) side open, thereby allowing Ca²⁺ influx. In such a cell, intracellular Ca²⁺ levels will rise both on the anodal side (as in B) and on the cathodal side, owing to depolarization-induced activation of the VGCCs. The direction of cell movement, if any, then depends on the balance between the opposing contractile forces.

Fig. 2. Various mechanisms that might underlie involvement of VGSCs in galvanotaxis. Contraction could be driven by  $ Ca^{2+} $ originating from a variety of sources secondary to  $ Na^{+} $ influx through VGSCs. Alternatively, it could be stimulated by protein kinase A (PKA) activated by cAMP, synthesized by adenylate cyclase, stimulated by  $ Na^{+} $. Direct interaction between the  $ \beta $ subunits of VGSCs and the cytoskeleton is also possible.
